Niacin metabolism. Niacin is derived from dietary sources and the cellular catabolism of tryptophan. As nicotinamide, niacin is the catalytic
moiety for nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP), which serve in multiple cellular
functions. In addition, oxidized NAD (NADþ) is utilized as a co-substrate in polyribosylation and sirtuin-related protein deacetylase reactions. Both
types of reactions are important in regulating a range of cellular functions. Moreover, NAD þ can be converted to cyclic ADP ribose (cADPR) or
adenosine diphosphate ribose (ADPR). ADPR and cADPR also act as cellular signaling molecules.

In this regard, vitamins required daily in millimolar amounts are usually less chemically stable, function in oxidative environments,
or are involved in numerous reactions. In addition, such vitamins often exist in tissues as dissociable cofactors. In contrast, vitamins
required daily in micromolar amounts are usually engaged in fewer reactions. They are also more likely to be bonded covalently to
the proteins they serve as cofactors or signaling molecules. Moreover, if their function is cell signaling, as few as 1000 molecules or
less may initiate an event (Rucker and Steinberg, 2002).
